stem: A 20-year-old man notices cola-colored urine starting the day after the onset of a sore throat. It cleared in 3 days, and this is the third such episode in 2 years. His blood pressure is 138/86 mm Hg. Urinalysis shows red cell casts and mild proteinuria. He has no edema, cough or hemoptysis.
oneliner: 20M + cola urine 1 day after each sore throat, 3rd episode + RBC casts + mild proteinuria + no edema or hemoptysis → which biopsy IF finding?
ask: Which renal biopsy immunofluorescence finding is most likely?

options.A: Granular IgG and C3 in subepithelial humps
options.B: Granular subepithelial IgG along the GBM
options.E: Granular IgA deposits in the mesangium

whyNot.A: Post-streptococcal humps; that disease starts **1 to 3 weeks after** a sore throat and rarely recurs, but his bleeding **starts the next day**
whyNot.B: Membranous nephropathy, which causes **nephrotic syndrome** with edema; he has **no edema** and only mild proteinuria
whyNot.C: Anti-GBM disease causes **rapidly progressive** renal failure, not brief episodes that **clear in 3 days**
whyNot.D: Minimal change disease shows no deposits, but it causes **heavy proteinuria and edema** without **red cell casts**

why: **IgA nephropathy** causes recurrent gross hematuria **during or within 1 to 2 days of a mucosal infection**, when increased galactose-deficient IgA1 deposits in the mesangium. **Post-streptococcal GN** has a **1 to 3 week latent period** after pharyngitis. Biopsy shows **mesangial IgA** deposits.

idea.rule: Hematuria at the time of the infection = IgA nephropathy (mesangial IgA); hematuria weeks later = post-infectious GN.
also: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein): same mesangial IgA with purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain
Post-streptococcal GN: low C3, subepithelial humps, anti-DNase B
IgA nephropathy: C3 usually normal
Post-streptococcal latency is about 1 to 3 weeks after pharyngitis and 3 to 6 weeks after skin infection

stem: A 47-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy and pitting leg edema starts furosemide. Seven days later, with the last dose taken 2 days ago, she feels weak and light-headed. Her blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. Serum Na+ is 130 mEq/L, urea nitrogen has risen from 25 to 85 mg/dL and creatinine from 1.8 to 2.2 mg/dL. A urine sample is examined.
oneliner: 47F + cardiomyopathy + edema + furosemide, last dose 2 days ago + BP 96/60 + Na 130 + BUN 25 → 85, creatinine 1.8 → 2.2 → which urine findings?
ask: Which urine findings are most likely?

options.A: Fractional excretion of Na+ above 2% with muddy brown granular casts
options.B: Red cell casts with dysmorphic red cells
options.C: Fractional excretion of Na+ below 1%, concentrated urine, no casts
options.E: Urine osmolality below 300 mOsm/kg with fractional excretion of Na+ above 2%

whyNot.A: **Acute tubular necrosis** keeps BUN:creatinine near 10-15; hers is about **39** (85/2.2), the prerenal pattern
whyNot.B: **Glomerulonephritis** gives a nephritic picture with hypertension; her BP is **96/60** after diuresis
whyNot.D: **Interstitial nephritis** damages tubules, so BUN:creatinine would not reach about **39**; no fever or rash is described
whyNot.E: Dilute, salt-wasting urine means damaged tubules or a diuretic still acting; her last dose was **2 days ago** and BUN:creatinine is about 39

answer: Low FENa, concentrated urine and a bland sediment (prerenal azotemia)
why: Over-diuresis drops perfusion, but the **tubules are intact**, so they reabsorb Na+ and water avidly: **FENa below 1%**, concentrated urine and a **bland sediment**. Urea is reabsorbed more than creatinine, so **BUN:creatinine exceeds 20**.

idea.rule: Prerenal azotemia: intact tubules save salt and water, so FENa is under 1%, urine is concentrated, the sediment is bland and BUN:creatinine exceeds 20.
also: Heart failure with low forward flow, as here before diuresis
Hemorrhage or vomiting with volume loss
Hepatorenal syndrome, where FENa is also below 1%
While a diuretic is still acting FENa is falsely high; fractional excretion of urea below 35% then shows the prerenal state

stem: A 64-year-old woman with end-stage kidney disease has missed her last two dialysis sessions and has deep, rapid breathing. Serum Na+ is 138 mEq/L, K+ 5.6 mEq/L, Cl- 98 mEq/L and HCO3- 14 mEq/L. Urea nitrogen is 96 mg/dL and creatinine 7.9 mg/dL. Arterial pH is 7.32 and PCO2 28 mm Hg. Serum ketones and lactate are normal.
oneliner: 64F + ESKD, missed 2 dialysis sessions + deep rapid breathing + Na 138, Cl 98, HCO3 14 + pH 7.32, PCO2 28 + no ketones, normal lactate → which acid-base reading?
ask: Which acid-base reading (anion gap and compensation) fits?

options.A: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
options.B: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with concurrent respiratory acidosis
options.C: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with concurrent respiratory alkalosis
options.D: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation

whyNot.A: Her anion gap is 138 - 98 - 14 = **26**, well above normal
whyNot.B: Respiratory acidosis needs a PCO2 **above** the expected value; Winter's formula gives 1.5 x 14 + 8 = 29 ± 2, and hers is 28
whyNot.C: That needs a PCO2 **below** 27; hers (28) sits inside the expected 27 to 31 range
whyNot.E: pH 7.32 and HCO3- 14 are **acidotic**, and her PCO2 is low, not raised

answer: High anion gap acidosis, respiratory compensation appropriate
why: The gap is **26** (retained phosphate, sulfate and other uremic anions), and **Winter's formula** (1.5 x HCO3- + 8 = 29 ± 2) predicts a PCO2 of 27 to 31. Her measured **28** falls inside, so compensation is appropriate and there is no second respiratory disorder.

idea.rule: Anion gap = Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-); expected PCO2 = 1.5 x HCO3- + 8 (±2). Higher PCO2 means added respiratory acidosis; lower means added respiratory alkalosis.
also: Gap above 12 in metabolic acidosis: MUDPILES causes (methanol, uremia, DKA, propylene glycol, lactate, ethylene glycol, salicylates)
Normal-gap acidosis from diarrhea or renal tubular acidosis has a gap near 8 to 12
Salicylate toxicity often adds a primary respiratory alkalosis
Delta gap against delta HCO3- finds a hidden second metabolic disorder

stem: A 17-year-old girl is brought in by her mother because of restrictive eating, fatigue and muscle cramps. Serum K+ is 2.3 mEq/L, Cl- 88 mEq/L and HCO3- 35 mEq/L; arterial pH is 7.49 and PCO2 49 mm Hg. She denies vomiting, her stools are normal, and her teeth and knuckles are normal. She has been secretly taking a pill every morning, and urine is collected 3 hours after the dose.
oneliner: 17F + restrictive eating + cramps + K 2.3, Cl 88, HCO3 35, pH 7.49, PCO2 49 + no vomiting, normal stools, teeth and knuckles + secret morning pill, urine 3 h after dose → which urine electrolytes?
ask: Which set of urine electrolytes is most likely?

options.A: Urine Cl- low, Na+ low, K+ high
options.B: Urine Cl- high, Na+ high, K+ high
options.C: Urine Cl- low, Na+ high, K+ high
options.D: Urine Cl- low, Na+ low, K+ low
options.E: Urine Cl- high, Na+ high, K+ low

whyNot.A: Chloride is low when the kidney is **saving** it, as after vomiting; the pill taken 3 hours ago would still be making her kidneys waste salt
whyNot.C: This early-vomiting pattern needs a **vomiting history**, which she denies; here the urine should be high in all three
whyNot.D: Low urine K+ means the K+ is lost **outside the kidney**; with no vomiting and normal stools there is no gut loss, so the kidney is the leak
whyNot.E: A pill acting on the kidney 3 hours ago sends more Na+ downstream and raises aldosterone, so urine K+ is **high**, not low

answer: Urine Cl-, Na+ and K+ all high (diuretic still acting)
why: A hypokalemic, hypochloremic **metabolic alkalosis** in someone who denies vomiting fits a **loop or thiazide diuretic**. While the drug acts, the kidney wastes Cl-, Na+ and K+, so **urine Cl- is above 20 mEq/L**; in vomiting, urine Cl- is **below 20**.

idea.rule: In hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, urine chloride above 20 mEq/L points to ongoing diuretic use (or Bartter/Gitelman, hyperaldosteronism); below 20 points to vomiting.
also: Vomiting: low urine Cl- (saline-responsive)
Bartter syndrome (loop-like) and Gitelman syndrome (thiazide-like): high urine Cl-
Primary hyperaldosteronism: high urine Cl- with hypertension
Remote diuretic use can give a low urine Cl- once the drug has worn off

stem: A 6-year-old boy has had dark, tea-colored urine and puffy eyelids on waking for 3 days. He had a sore throat 2 weeks ago. His blood pressure is 134/88 mm Hg, he has passed little urine today, and he has no fever or flank pain. Urine microscopy is performed.
oneliner: 6M + dark urine + puffy eyelids + sore throat 2 weeks ago + BP 134/88 + low urine output, afebrile, no flank pain → which urine microscopy finding?
ask: Which urine microscopy finding is most likely?

options.D: Red cells of normal shape without casts
options.E: Red cell casts with dysmorphic red cells

whyNot.A: These suggest **pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis**; he has no fever or flank pain
whyNot.B: These mark **acute tubular necrosis** after an ischemic or toxic insult; his picture is nephritic, with edema and hypertension
whyNot.C: Broad waxy casts reflect **advanced chronic kidney disease**, not a child ill for 3 days
whyNot.D: This points to bleeding **below the glomerulus**, as from a stone; his edema, BP 134/88 and falling urine output indicate glomerular disease

answer: Red cell casts with dysmorphic red cells (glomerular bleeding)
why: Edema, hypertension and falling output after a sore throat make **post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis**. Red cells squeezed through damaged glomeruli become **dysmorphic** and molded into **red cell casts**, which localize bleeding to the glomerulus.

idea.rule: Red cell casts and dysmorphic red cells put the bleeding in the glomerulus; red cells without casts suggest a lower-tract or stone source.
also: White cell casts: pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis
Muddy brown granular casts: acute tubular necrosis
Fatty casts and oval fat bodies: nephrotic syndrome
Hyaline casts: concentrated urine or dehydration, can be normal
